{{Short description|Sphere with radius one, usually centered on the origin of the space}}
[[File:Unit disc 2-norm qtl1.svg|thumb|Unit ball (red) and unit sphere (blue) for the Euclidean norm in two dimensions.]]

In [[mathematics]], a '''unit sphere''' is a [[sphere]] of unit [[radius]]: the [[locus (mathematics)|set of points]] at [[Euclidean distance]] [[1]] from some [[center (geometry)|center point]] in [[three-dimensional space]]. More generally, the ''unit {{tmath|n}}-sphere'' is an [[n-sphere|{{tmath|n}}-sphere]] of unit radius in {{tmath|(n+1)}}-[[dimension]]al [[Euclidean space]]; the [[unit circle]] is a special case, the unit {{tmath|1}}-sphere in the [[Euclidean plane|plane]]. An ([[Open set|open]]) '''unit ball''' is the region inside of a unit sphere, the set of points of distance less than 1 from the center.

A unit sphere or unit ball with center at the [[origin (mathematics)|origin]] of the space is called ''the'' (canonical) unit sphere or ''the'' (canonical) unit ball. Any arbitrary sphere can be transformed to the unit sphere by a combination of [[translation (geometry)|translation]] and [[scaling (geometry)|scaling]], so the study of spheres in general can often be reduced to the study of the unit sphere.

The unit sphere is often used as a model for [[spherical geometry]] because it has constant [[sectional curvature]] of 1, which simplifies calculations. In [[trigonometry]], circular [[arc length]] on the unit circle is called [[radian]]s and used for measuring [[angular distance]]; in [[spherical trigonometry]] surface area on the unit sphere is called [[steradian]]s and used for measuring [[solid angle]].

In more general contexts, a ''unit sphere'' is the set of points of [[distance]] 1 from a fixed central point, where different [[norm (mathematics)|norms]] can be used as general notions of "distance", and an (open) ''unit ball'' is the region inside.
[[File:Vector norms.svg|frame|right|Some 1-spheres: {{math|‖'''x'''‖<sub>2</sub>}} is the norm for Euclidean space.]]

== Unit spheres and balls in Euclidean space ==

In [[Euclidean space]] of {{tmath|n}} dimensions, the {{tmath|(n-1)}}-dimensional unit sphere is the set of all points <math>(x_1, \ldots, x_n)</math> which satisfy the equation
<math display=block>x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \cdots + x_n ^2 = 1.</math>

The open unit {{tmath|n}}-ball is the set of all points satisfying the [[inequality (mathematics)|inequality]]
<math display=block>x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \cdots + x_n ^2 < 1,</math>
and closed unit {{tmath|n}}-ball is the set of all points satisfying the inequality
<math display=block>x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \cdots + x_n ^2 \le 1.</math>

=== Volume and area ===
{{see also|Volume of an n-ball}}
[[File:Graphs of volumes (V) and surface areas (S) of n-balls of radius 1.png|thumb|right|Graphs of volumes ({{mvar|V}}) and surface areas ({{mvar|S}}) of unit {{mvar|n}}-balls]]

The classical equation of a unit sphere is that of the ellipsoid with a radius of 1 and no alterations to the {{tmath|x}}-, {{tmath|y}}-, or {{tmath|z}}- axes:
<math display=block>x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1</math>

The volume of the unit ball in Euclidean {{tmath|n}}-space, and the surface area of the unit sphere, appear in many important formulas of [[mathematical analysis|analysis]].  The volume of the unit {{tmath|n}}-ball, which we denote <math>V_n,</math> can be expressed by making use of the [[gamma function]].  It is
<math display=block>V_n = \frac{\pi ^ {n/2}}{\Gamma(1+n/2)} = \begin{cases}
{\pi^{n/2}}/{(n/2)!} & \mathrm{if~}n \ge 0\mathrm{~is~even} \\[6mu]
{2(2\pi)^{(n-1)/2}}/{n!!} & \mathrm{if~}n \ge 0\mathrm{~is~odd,}
\end{cases} </math>
where <math>n!!</math> is the [[double factorial]].

The hypervolume of the {{tmath|(n-1)}}-dimensional unit sphere (''i.e.'', the "area" of the boundary of the {{tmath|n}}-dimensional unit ball), which we denote <math>A_{n-1},</math> can be expressed as
<math display=block>A_{n-1} = n V_n = \frac{n \pi ^ {n/2}}{\Gamma(1+n/2)} = \frac{2 \pi ^ {n/2}}{\Gamma(n/2)} = \begin{cases}
{2 \pi^{n/2}}/{(n/2 - 1)!} & \mathrm{if~}n \ge 1\mathrm{~is~even} \\[6mu]
{2(2\pi)^{(n-1)/2}}/{(n-2)!!} & \mathrm{if~}n \ge 1\mathrm{~is~odd.}
\end{cases}</math>
For example, <math>A_0 = 2</math> is the "area" of the boundary of the unit ball <math>[-1,1] \subset \mathbb{R}</math>, which simply counts the two points. Then <math>A_1 = 2\pi</math> is the "area" of the boundary of the unit disc, which is the circumference of the unit circle. <math>A_2 = 4\pi</math> is the area of the boundary of the unit ball <math>\{ x \in \R^3 : x_1^2 + x_2^2 + x_3^2 \leq 1 \}</math>, which is the surface area of the unit sphere <math>\{ x \in \R^3 : x_1^2 + x_2^2 + x_3^2 = 1 \}</math>.

The surface areas and the volumes for some values of {{tmath|n}} are as follows:

==== Recursion ====

The <math>A_n</math> values satisfy the recursion:
<math display=block>A_0 = 2</math>
<math display=block>A_1 = 2\pi</math>
<math display=block>A_n = \frac{2 \pi}{n-1} A_{n-2}</math> for {{tmath|n > 1}}.

The <math>V_n</math> values satisfy the recursion:
<math display=block>V_0 = 1</math>
<math display=block>V_1 = 2</math>
<math display=block>V_n = \frac{2 \pi}{n} V_{n-2}</math> for {{tmath|n > 1}}.

==== Non-negative real-valued dimensions ====
{{Main|Hausdorff measure}}

The value <math display=inline>2^{-n} V_n = \pi ^ {n/2} \big/\, 2^n \Gamma\bigl(1+\tfrac12n\bigr)</math> at non-negative real values of {{tmath|n}} is sometimes used for normalization of Hausdorff measure.<ref>[https://www.math.cuhk.edu.hk/course_builder/1415/math5011/MATH5011_Chapter_3.2014.pdf The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Math 5011, Chapter 3, Lebesgue and Hausdorff Measures]</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last = Manin | first = Yuri I. | author-link = | title = The notion of dimension in geometry and algebra | journal = Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society | volume = 43 | issue = 2 | pages = 139–161 | date = 2006| language = | url = https://www.ams.org/bull/2006-43-02/S0273-0979-06-01081-0/S0273-0979-06-01081-0.pdf | jstor = | issn = | doi = 10.1090/S0273-0979-06-01081-0| id = | mr = | zbl = | jfm = | access-date = 17 December 2021}}</ref>

==== Other radii ====
{{Main|N-sphere#Volume and area}}

The surface area of an {{tmath|(n-1)}}-sphere with radius {{tmath|r}} is <math>A_{n-1} r^{n-1}</math> and the volume of an {{tmath|n}}-ball with radius {{tmath|r}} is <math>V_{n} r^{n}.</math>  For instance, the area is <math>A_2 = 4\pi r^2</math> for the two-dimensional surface of the three-dimensional ball of radius <math>r.</math>  The volume is <math>V_3 = \tfrac43\pi r^3</math> for the three-dimensional ball of radius&nbsp;{{tmath|r}}.

== Unit balls in normed vector spaces ==

The '''open unit ball''' of a [[normed vector space]] {{tmath|V}} with the [[Norm (mathematics)|norm]] <math>\|\cdot\|</math> is given by
<math display=block>\{ x\in V: \|x\|<1 \}</math>

It is the [[interior (topology)|topological interior]] of the '''closed unit ball''' of <math>(V, \|\cdot\|)\colon</math>
<math display=block>\{ x\in V: \|x\|\le 1\}</math>

The latter is the disjoint union of the former and their common border, the '''unit sphere''' of <math>(V, \|\cdot\|)\colon</math>
<math display=block>\{ x\in V: \|x\| = 1 \}</math>

The "shape" of the ''unit ball'' is entirely dependent on the chosen norm; it may well have "corners", and for example may look like <math>[-1,1]^n</math> in the case of the max-norm in {{tmath|\mathbb{R}^n}}. One obtains a naturally ''round ball'' as the unit ball pertaining to the usual [[Hilbert space]] norm, based in the finite-dimensional case on the [[Euclidean distance]]; its boundary is what is usually meant by the ''unit sphere''.

Let  <math>x=(x_1,...x_n)\in \R^n.</math> Define the usual {{tmath|\ell_p}}-norm for <math>p \ge 1</math> as:
<math display=block>\|x\|_p = \biggl(\sum_{k=1}^n |x_k|^p \biggr)^{1/p}</math>

Then <math>\|x\|_2</math> is the usual [[Hilbert space]] norm.
<math>\|x\|_1</math> is called the Hamming norm, or {{tmath|\ell_1}}-norm.
The condition <math>p \geq 1</math> is necessary in the definition of the <math>\ell_p</math> norm, as the unit ball in any normed space must be [[convex set|convex]] as a consequence of the [[triangle inequality]].
Let <math>\|x\|_\infty</math> denote the max-norm or {{tmath|\ell_\infty}}-norm of {{tmath|x}}.

Note that for the one-dimensional circumferences <math>C_p</math> of the two-dimensional unit balls, we have:
<math display=block>C_{1} = 4 \sqrt{2}</math> is the minimum value.
<math display=block>C_{2} = 2 \pi</math>
<math display=block>C_{\infty} = 8</math> is the maximum value.

== Generalizations ==

=== Metric spaces ===
All three of the above definitions can be straightforwardly generalized to a [[metric space]], with respect to a chosen origin. However, topological considerations (interior, closure, border) need not apply in the same way (e.g., in [[ultrametric]] spaces, all of the three are simultaneously open and closed sets), and the unit sphere may even be empty in some metric spaces.

=== Quadratic forms ===
If {{tmath|V}} is a linear space with a real [[quadratic form]] <math>F : V \to \R,</math> then <math>\{ p \in V : F(p) = 1\}</math> may be called the unit sphere<ref>Takashi Ono (1994) ''Variations on a Theme of Euler: quadratic forms, elliptic curves, and Hopf maps'', chapter 5: Quadratic spherical maps, page 165, [[Plenum Press]], {{isbn|0-306-44789-4}}</ref><ref>F. Reese Harvey (1990) ''Spinors and calibrations'', "Generalized Spheres", page 42, [[Academic Press]], {{isbn|0-12-329650-1}}</ref> or [[hyperboloid#Relation to the sphere|unit quasi-sphere]] of <math>V.</math> For example, the quadratic form {{tmath|x^2 - y^2}}, when set equal to one, produces the [[unit hyperbola]], which plays the role of the "unit circle" in the plane of [[split-complex number]]s. Similarly, the quadratic form <math>x^2</math> yields a pair of lines for the unit sphere in the [[dual number]] plane.
